content: The comments provided by over 100 reviewers were carefully considered and incorporated into the revised guidelines wherever feasible. Since 2008, the World Health Organization (WHO) has adopted the GRADE system for evaluating the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. The GRADE system distinctly separates the assessment of evidence quality from the strength of recommendations. Evidence quality is defined as the confidence that the reported estimates of effect are sufficient to support a specific recommendation. Randomized controlled trials are initially rated as high-quality evidence but may be downgraded due to factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency of results across studies, indirectness of evidence, imprecision, and publication bias. Conversely, observational studies are initially rated as low-quality evidence but may be upgraded if the treatment effect is very large, if multiple studies demonstrate consistent effects, if there is evidence of a dose-response relationship, or if all plausible biases would underestimate the effect. The higher the quality of evidence, the more likely a strong recommendation can be made. The strength of a recommendation reflects the confidence of the Guideline Development Group that the desirable effects of following a recommendation outweigh the potential undesirable effects. The GRADE system classifies recommendations as either strong or conditional. A strong recommendation indicates high confidence that the desirable effects of adherence outweigh the undesirable effects. A conditional recommendation suggests that the desirable effects probably outweigh the undesirable effects, but there is less certainty about these trade-offs. The reasons for making a conditional recommendation include the absence of high-quality evidence, imprecision in outcome estimates, variability in individual values and preferences, small benefits, limited applicability across all settings, or benefits that may not justify the costs, including implementation costs. Key domains considered in determining the strength of recommendations include the balance of benefits and risks, values and preferences, costs and financial implications, and feasibility. Strong recommendations are more likely when benefits clearly outweigh risks, when the recommendation is widely acceptable or highly valued, when costs are lower or cost-effectiveness is greater, and when the intervention is feasible in the settings where it is most needed. The guidelines will be disseminated both as printed publications and electronically on the WHO website in six official United Nations languages. The web version will include all annexes, and a shorter version will summarize key new and existing recommendations for easy reference. A library of supporting documentation and evidence will also be made available online. WHO headquarters will collaborate with regional and country offices and implementing partners to ensure wide dissemination through regional and subregional meetings. Assistance will be provided to Member States to adapt the guidelines to their national contexts. An evaluation framework has been developed to assess the uptake of the recommendations and identify barriers to effective implementation. A review of the guidelines is planned for 2015, with interim updates to be issued if significant new evidence becomes available. The guidelines include recommendations for specific populations, such as adults, pregnant and breastfeeding women, adolescents, children, and key populations. These populations are clearly specified for each recommendation and marked with appropriate symbols for quick reference. Key populations include vulnerable and most-at-risk groups, such as men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, people who inject drugs, and sex workers. The use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in key populations should follow the same general principles and recommendations as for adults. Specific recommendations for community-based HIV testing are included for key populations. Adolescents with HIV include those surviving perinatal infection and those newly acquiring infection through sexual activity, injecting drug use, unsafe injections, or blood transfusions. Adolescents may access care in various settings, including pediatric, antenatal, and adult clinics. However, the lack of adolescent-specific services in many health systems poses challenges for accessing care and maintaining adherence to treatment regimens. Clinical and general care recommendations for adults generally apply to adolescents, with specific guidance for adolescents indicated where relevant. The guidelines emphasize the importance of early HIV testing and counseling as a gateway to treatment, care, and prevention. Globally, it is estimated that about half of people living with HIV are unaware of their status. Many individuals test late, and poor linkage from testing to care—such as delays in assessing ART eligibility—results in late treatment initiation, poor health outcomes, and ongoing HIV transmission. The goal of national HIV programs should be to identify people living with HIV as early as possible after infection and link them promptly to prevention, care, and treatment services. Those who test negative should also be linked to appropriate prevention services.
